name: Push/pull/legs (PPL)

lead: Push/pull/legs, or PPL, divides weekly weight training into a push day (chest, shoulders, triceps), a pull day (back, biceps) and a leg day. It is one of several common splits alongside full-body, upper/lower and the bro split, and lifters use it to build a muscular physique.

A split spreads weekly training volume across muscle groups and days. Run twice through a week, PPL hits each muscle about twice. Research summarised on Wikipedia reports that with equal volume, frequency did not change strength gains, and for muscle growth two sessions per week produced greater effects than one. No comparative research on PPL versus other splits is cited.

paras: People run it as three days on a rotating schedule or as six days a week, with rest days placed where recovery needs them. It is commonly paired with progressive overload and a calorie surplus when the goal is size. Visible changes build over months.
No harms specific to PPL are documented. General resistance-training cautions apply, such as overtraining from excessive volume, and the six-day version leaves less rest time between sessions.

angle.text: A popular weekly split for building a muscular physique, with each muscle trained about twice a week across push, pull and leg days. More frequent work per muscle spreads volume across the week toward steady growth. Research on frequency shows two weekly sessions produced greater muscle growth than one.

lead: Push/pull/legs (PPL) is a training split that divides weekly resistance training into push, pull and leg days. Wikipedia defines a split as how a trainee divides weekly training volume across muscle groups and days, and lists push/pull/legs among common splits [1].
The wiki treats it as a routine structure popular in lifting communities. The structure itself is documented only briefly in encyclopedias, and no comparative studies of splits are cited there [1].
Research summarised alongside it concerns frequency and volume in general, which are the variables a split changes.
infobox: Push session, pull session, leg session

paras: Wikipedia lists full body, upper/lower, push/pull/legs and the bro split as common splits, and notes that some programs alternate splits from week to week [1]. In a PPL arrangement, pushing movements (and the muscles they train) are grouped on one day, pulling on another, and leg training on a third.

Per Wikipedia's summary, more weekly sessions generally produce larger strength gains, but when total volume is equalized frequency had no influence on strength [1][2]. For muscle growth, two sessions per week produced greater effects than one, and whether three beats two remains unresolved [1][2]. Training volume is described as one of the most critical variables [1].
No studies found comparing push/pull/legs directly with other splits in the material reviewed. Related research on training frequency and volume is summarised above [1][2].
